expectations.text: All workers are spawned in a single message (single Task tool invocation batch) — NOT spawned sequentially one at a time
expectations.evidence: The transcript explicitly states: 'No sub-agents were spawned.' and 'No multi-agent research pipeline was used.' Zero Task tool calls were made. The report was generated directly from the model's training knowledge in a single LLM call with no worker spawning at all.

expectations.text: Spawns 2-3 workers — one per comparison dimension (PostgreSQL, MySQL, benchmarks/cases)
expectations.evidence: Transcript confirms: 'No sub-agents were spawned.' No workers of any kind were created. The transcript notes this was done entirely without the deep-research skill or any multi-agent workflow.

expectations.text: Report covers both PostgreSQL AND MySQL with equivalent depth — neither is treated as an afterthought
expectations.evidence: The report.md covers both databases across 9 dimensions (Architecture, Performance, Replication/HA, Features, Ecosystem, Operations, Licensing, Decision Guide, Scorecard). Each dimension provides subsections for both PostgreSQL and MySQL with comparable detail. The summary scorecard evaluates both across 13 categories. Neither database is an afterthought.

expectations.text: Cross-References section identifies at least one real disagreement or nuance between sources (e.g., MySQL faster for simple reads vs PostgreSQL better for complex queries)
expectations.evidence: There is no 'Cross-References' section and no external sources were consulted. The transcript explicitly states: 'No external sources were consulted.' While the report does note performance nuances (e.g., 'For pure high-throughput OLTP... both are competitive', 'MySQL InnoDB historically had lower write amplification'), these are not sourced disagreements between references — they are unsupported claims from training data.

expectations.text: Bibliography includes at least 3 sources dated 2023 or later, or sources that discuss recent versions (PostgreSQL 15+, MySQL 8+)
expectations.evidence: No bibliography exists in the report. The transcript confirms: 'No external sources were consulted.' The report ends with a disclaimer: 'This report is based on knowledge current through early 2025 and general industry trends.' While the report mentions PostgreSQL 15/16 and MySQL 8.x in the text, these are not cited references.

expectations.text: Conclusions section includes a clear recommendation (or decision framework) for when to choose PostgreSQL vs MySQL — not 'it depends' without criteria
expectations.evidence: Section 8 'When to Choose Each' lists concrete criteria for each database (e.g., 'Choose PostgreSQL when: complex queries, JSONB, pgvector, PostGIS, open-source governance...' and 'Choose MySQL when: Vitess sharding, existing MySQL codebase, WordPress/PHP ecosystem...'). The Conclusion section gives a direct verdict: 'PostgreSQL is the default recommendation for new high-traffic web applications.' Clear criteria are provided, not a vague 'it depends.'

claims.claim: The report covers 9 major comparison dimensions
claims.evidence: Confirmed: Architecture and Concurrency, Performance at Scale, Replication and HA, Feature Richness, Ecosystem and Cloud Support, Operational Complexity, Licensing and Governance, When to Choose Each, Summary Scorecard — exactly 9 sections.
Transcript explicitly confirms: 'No web searches were performed.' and 'No external sources were consulted.'

claims.evidence: Unverifiable from available outputs — no external sources were consulted. This is a training-data claim that cannot be checked against current documentation in this run.

claims.evidence: Unverifiable — no sources cited. YouTube/Vitess is historically documented, but Slack and GitHub attributions cannot be verified without external sources.

claims.evidence: No sources cited to support the momentum claim. This is an assertion from training data without supporting evidence in the output.

workarounds: Entire report generated from model training data rather than live research — no web searches or agent spawning performed

suggestions.assertion: Report covers both PostgreSQL AND MySQL with equivalent depth — neither is treated as an afterthought
suggestions.reason: This assertion passes too easily. A report fabricated entirely from training data with no research can still satisfy 'equivalent depth' coverage. Consider adding a criterion that depth requires sourced evidence (e.g., at least 2 cited sources per database), which would distinguish genuine research from hallucinated equivalence.

suggestions.assertion: Conclusions section includes a clear recommendation (or decision framework) for when to choose PostgreSQL vs MySQL
suggestions.reason: This also passes for training-data output. Any sufficiently capable LLM can produce decision criteria without doing real research. Consider coupling this with a requirement that at least one criterion is supported by a cited source from 2023+, which would force the output to be grounded in evidence.

No assertion checks whether the report contains any actual benchmark numbers or data points (e.g., throughput figures, latency numbers, connection counts). The without_skill run makes general claims (e.g., 'PgBouncer is essentially required at 500+ connections') without citing data. An assertion like 'Report includes at least 2 quantitative benchmark data points from cited sources' would sharply differentiate researched vs. training-data outputs.

No assertion checks the total research effort (agent spawning, web searches performed). The 4 worker-spawning assertions (expectations 1-2) test the same failure mode twice and could be merged into one, freeing space for a more discriminating quality assertion.

eval_feedback.overall: The two hardest expectations (worker spawning, bibliography) correctly fail for baseline output. However, two expectations (coverage depth, decision framework) pass easily for training-data output — a sufficiently coherent LLM response can satisfy them without doing any actual research. Adding source-grounded variants of these assertions would make the eval more discriminating.
